title: The marketing automation model that drove 9x qualified lead growth in a secondary market
content:
When we reviewed our Japan marketing automation programs last year, the picture wasn’t pretty. Our automated emails were generating about 12 qualified leads per month against a goal of 160.
We could have done the obvious and by hiring a local marketing automation specialist in Japan. Instead, we rebuilt Japan’s entire email automation program in two months, with zero additional headcount, using a model any marketing team can replicate. Here’s what we learned.
HubSpot is a US-headquartered company. And like most US-headquartered companies, our marketing automation investment has historically been concentrated in a handful of core markets: English, French, Spanish, German, Portuguese. Those programs get built, refined, optimized, and rebuilt again. Markets outside that core group tend to get less dedicated attention, not because anyone decided to deprioritize them, but because the automation resources weren’t scoped to cover them.
For Japan, that meant automation programs that were years old, partially built, or never meaningfully localized. The content existed, and the infrastructure was there. But it wasn’t performing because it wasn’t designed for the Japanese market.
This is a pattern that shows up across companies operating in multiple regions. Wherever there’s a primary market and a secondary one, the secondary market tends to lag. That’s because the people with automation expertise are almost always scoped to the markets that generate the most volume.
Marketing automation in markets outside the core group tends to fall into one of two failure modes: it was never built, or it was built years ago and never meaningfully updated.
Japan was the second case. And the typical response, “we need to hire a local automation expert,” wasn’t realistic. What we needed was a different model.
We were asking the wrong question. Instead of “Who can own this end to end?”, we should have asked, “Should one person own this?”
Marketing automation has two fundamentally different jobs. One is technical : building journey logic, setting up workflows, defining enrollment criteria, creating segmentation, and configuring tracking. None of that requires speaking Japanese. The other job is cultural : making sure the message feels right, the tone lands, the pain points are real, the call-to-action makes sense. That absolutely requires someone who knows the market.
The mistake teams make is assuming both jobs need to live with one person. They don’t. When you separate them cleanly, you don’t need a local automation specialist. You need an automation marketer who understands the technical side, and a local marketing or sales partner who owns the cultural validation. Together, they cover everything.
With that model in place, here’s what two months of focused work produced for Japan:
Within the first reporting period, automation-sourced qualified leads jumped roughly 9x (from 12 to over 115 per month), making a significant contribution to Japan’s monthly qualified lead goal. We estimate that translates to about 44 incremental deals per month.
We deliberately focused on high-intent automation programs rather than trying to rebuild everything at once. Here’s why that paid off.
Treating all email programs the same kills most rebuilds before they start.
There are two types of automation programs: high-intent and low-intent. High-intent programs go to people who are already showing early buying signals: they’ve visited pricing pages, browsed product features, or taken actions that suggest they’re actively evaluating. Low-intent programs reach colder audiences through broad nurture flows.
High-intent programs have fewer emails, more focused messaging, and clear calls-to-action. They’re easier to localize, faster to build, and they convert. Low-intent programs have large email volumes, varied content, and much longer paths to conversion. They require significantly more localization work for a smaller payoff.
In Japan, our decision to start with high-intent trigger-based emails is the reason we saw 9x growth in qualified leads in two months instead of incremental improvement over a year.
Once we had one person owning the technical side and one person owning the cultural side, here’s how things played out day-to-day.
The regional marketing partner owned the following:
The regional partner didn’t write the emails from scratch. We used AI to produce first drafts, which they then refined and validated. Their job was cultural expertise rather than copywriting, which kept their time commitment to five days across the whole project.
We held firm on one principle: the regional partner must understand the local customer journey, not just the language. Translation alone isn’t enough. A native speaker who doesn’t know how Japanese SMBs evaluate software is not the right person for this role.
Before applying this approach to any market, we ran a simple go/no-go check. The model works when all of the following are true:
If your automation is already strong, don’t use this model. The incremental gain won’t justify the effort to rebuild. If you don’t have a local partner who genuinely understands the market, wait until you do. Language fluency alone will produce technically correct emails that don’t convert.
For teams that want to try this, here’s the process we’d use again:
Check how many active workflows exist for this region, whether email delivery volume has been declining year-over-year, and whether automation-sourced qualified leads are significantly below goal. Those signals tell you whether you’re doing a full build, a rebuild, or an expansion.
Multiply your high-intent audience size by your email-to-lead conversion rate. If the estimate is fewer than 20 incremental qualified leads per month, the project probably doesn’t justify the investment.
Ask two questions: Do they understand how customers in this market make buying decisions, beyond just the language? Can they commit roughly one day per program for QA and messaging review? A contractor counts. A translator alone does not.
Answer six questions with your local partner before writing a single email: Who is the primary audience? What are their three most urgent pain points? Which global messages resonate here, and which don’t? What tone is right? What proof points are most credible? What should you avoid? Both parties sign off before anything gets built.
The automation marketer reviews everything language-independent: journey structure, workflow logic, segmentation, performance data. The local partner reviews everything copy-dependent: subject lines, body copy, tone. Assign a verdict for each element: reuse, adapt, or rebuild.
Quick test: would this email make sense to send to someone who visited your pricing page today? If yes, build it first. Low-intent programs need more content and localization work for a smaller payoff. Layer them in once the foundation is live.
The automation marketer checks tokens, workflow logic, test send, suppression lists, and tracking. The local partner checks for natural language, appropriate tone, relevant pain points, and a clear CTA. Both sign off before launch.
Day 30: early signals only. Don’t optimize yet. Day 60: compare against baseline and adjust if needed. Day 90: full picture. Qualified lead volume, deals, contribution to goal, and a decision on whether to expand.
The Japan pilot proved something we now believe applies broadly: you don’t need a local automation specialist in every market. You need a clear split of responsibilities between someone who owns the technical infrastructure and someone who owns the cultural context.
That’s a much more achievable team structure than hiring specialized roles in every region. It’s also faster because both people can work simultaneously rather than sequentially.
The biggest risk is rushing past the cultural alignment step or treating QA as a translation proofread. Give your local partner real authority to validate the customer experience, and the results will follow.
We went from 12 qualified leads to 115 in two months, and we didn’t add headcount.

title: It’s Possible Your Migration Issues May Be Due To Site Quality via @sejournal, @marie_haynes
content:
There have been a number of reports recently of sites struggling to be properly indexed following a site migration.
I have consulted with a few sites on this issue and have developed a theory.
Please know that this theory is not something I can prove at this point. I am writing this blog post to generate discussion.
I believe that not only does a site migration trigger a new review of site quality from Google, but also that Google’s standards for site quality have become much stricter.
I was hired to do a site quality review for a site that blogs on a hobby topic. The site had previously performed well and was starting to see a slow decline over the last year or so. Just before I started my review, the site owner reached out to tell me that they had just started migrating to a new domain.
From what I can see, they did everything correctly. They submitted the change of address in Google Search Console , carefully mapped redirects, updated internal links, ensured Google could crawl the new site, and generated a sitemap for the new domain.
In the Page Indexing Report, 98% of their URLs were reported as not indexed.
Even worse, inspecting any page, including those 33 pages that Google said were indexed showed the same thing. The page was indeed not indexed. Google had classified it as “ crawled – currently not indexed .”
There wasn’t a problem with Google finding the new page. Rather, they had crawled it and chosen not to index it.
We ran a live test in GSC on several of these pages. In each case the report told us the page was available to be indexing, but only if certain conditions were met.
That link points to this page in which Google tells us the page might not get indexed if it is subject to a manual action or a duplicate of another page. Neither of these was the case. We wondered if the site migration caused duplication issues. But Google clearly recognized the canonical as this new site, and the old page was properly redirecting to it.
However, Google lists a third possible reason for not indexing a valid page: The page quality must be high enough to warrant indexing.
In my review for this site, I noted that while the site was well written and thorough, there was very little original value on any page compared to what already exists on other sites on the web.
They were all commodity content – content that is essentially the same across other sites on the internet.
Google recently updated its documentation on creating helpful content to include new information on the “main content” of your webpage. The main content is the part of the page that helps fulfil the searcher’s need. In it, they emphasized the importance of:
That point on originality is what I think matters most here. Google describes it as “The extent to which the content offers unique, original information or perspectives that aren’t already available on other websites.”
This is the obvious question! Why was the quality acceptable on the old domain and suddenly deemed low quality after the migration?
I think that if Google applied these quality standards across the board to every site on the internet, the vast majority of websites would suffer catastrophic loss. Who knows, it is possible we will see this with a future core update.
My theory is that when the site I reviewed migrated to a new domain, this triggered a more strict quality assessment. Given that none of the pages offered information that truly was original and offered more than what is already available on other websites, Google’s systems decided not to index it.
If you cannot get indexed following a site migration, first you should thoroughly review for technical reasons. Ensure you have properly redirected old pages to new. Make sure you record the change of address in Google Search Console. Use the Live Test in GSC to verify that Google can see the content on these pages. It is a good idea to connect with an SEO who can thoroughly investigate technical issues.
It’s also worth knowing that site migrations can take time for Google to process . It is possible you just need to wait longer . In the case I mentioned above, however, it has been four months now, and only the homepage is indexed. There is definitely something wrong.
If it is indeed an issue with site quality , then I would suggest producing a small handful of truly original and insightful articles. For many sites, this requires a whole new business direction. It’s no longer good enough to write about things the world already knows. You need to find things you can create that bring something new to the internet that people will find of value.
What I don’t know, however, is whether Google will consider the value of these individual pages or whether your overall site quality score, diminished because of unoriginal content, will hinder indexing of these pages as well.
Another option to consider is to start completely over on a new domain with brand new content. I realize this is not the answer you are looking for. However, if my theory is right, then there is no technical SEO fix for many of these sites that are struggling to get their new domain indexed.

title: Google Takes Applications For A UGC Pipeline Separate From Crawling via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
content:
For most websites, crawling is still how you get into Google Search. Googlebot finds a URL and retrieves the page; then, independently, Google’s systems determine if they want to add this page to their index.
On Oct. 8, Google added Search Central documentation describing how approved forums and social platforms can submit user-generated content directly to Google.
The UGC Fresh Data Program allows approved platforms to submit content and interaction signals through a “dedicated data ingestion pipeline” that accepts data submission from those platforms. Google states that the pipeline is separate from both traditional crawlers and the Indexing API. According to Google, participation in the UGC Fresh Data Program does not ensure your content will be included in Google Search.
Google has partnered with individual social platforms before, including Twitter in 2009 and Reddit in 2024. This time the criteria are posted and there’s an application form , so you can check most of Google’s requirements against a platform’s own pages before applying. The form asks how many monthly active users the platform has and when it launched.
The Search Central documentation changelog links to the page under the entry for Oct. 8: “Added documentation on the UGC Fresh Data Program.” Google wrote that the page is meant to explain the program’s purpose and help applicants “understand the eligibility criteria and how to participate.”
The UGC Fresh Data Program is an initiative designed to help platforms display fresh, high quality, and authentic user-generated content (UGC) across various features on Search.
Google says sending content through the pipeline “helps ensure that fresh content is processed and quickly updated in Search.” The page gives no time frame for “quickly.” It also says the program “doesn’t guarantee that content will appear in Search.”
The page limits the program to “trending UGC content.” It describes the pipeline as “independent of the Google Indexing API and traditional organic crawling for general web content.”
Oct. 8 is when the page went up. Neither the page nor the changelog entry says when the pipeline started operating.
Submitting an application “doesn’t guarantee participation,” according to the page, and Google will share developer documents “once accepted into the program.”
The form has seven required fields: company name, service domain, 10 sample URLs with UGC, monthly active users, launch date, a Search Console owner’s email and a contact email. It calls a submission “merely an expression of interest” and says Google “has no obligation to incorporate your content in our features.”
The form goes further than the page on where content could show up, saying submitted content “is eligible to serve on Google Search and other surfaces, especially for time-sensitive or fresh content.” It adds, “we never guarantee serving as that is determined entirely by ranking algorithms.”
Any site can ask Google to crawl its pages, according to Google’s recrawl documentation . Owners and full users of a Search Console property can request crawls of individual URLs in the URL Inspection tool, within a quota, and sitemaps cover larger sets of URLs. Google says crawling “can take anywhere from a few days to a few weeks,” and that a request “does not guarantee that inclusion in search results will happen instantly or even at all.”
The Indexing API is narrower. It covers pages with JobPosting, or BroadcastEvent embedded in a VideoObject, and lets their owners tell Google when a page is added, updated or removed. This “allows Google to schedule pages for a fresh crawl.” There is a “default 200 quota” available for API onboarding and submission testing; however, the API “requires additional approval for usage and resource provisioning.” In a September post I noted several job boards had gone months without a reply to their approval requests.
Recrawls, sitemaps, the Indexing API provide the URL for crawling. Platforms submit what Google calls “content and interaction signals” through the UGC program, but this does not replace public URLs. The criteria still require that the content be accessible via Googlebot.
The Indexing API has a default quota for onboarding and testing, with additional approval required for further usage. The UGC program requires Google to approve applicants. Neither guarantees that submitted content will appear in Search. Of the three options being compared here, recrawl requests and sitemaps do not include a request for approval. The program’s “within minutes” wording covers sending, not indexing.
On Dec. 7, 2009, Google launched real-time search results that showed “live updates from people on popular sites like Twitter and FriendFeed.” The post named Facebook, MySpace, FriendFeed, Jaiku and Identi.ca as new partners, along with Twitter, which Google said it had announced “a few weeks ago.”
In July 2011, Google said “that agreement expired on July 2,” as Datamation reported at the time. In May 2015, Google said it was bringing Tweets to Search on mobile, and it added desktop that August.
In February 2024, Google stated that it “now has access” to Reddit’s Data API . According to Google, this Data API delivers “real-time, structured, unique content.” Google noted that accessing the Data API would provide “enhanced signals that will help us better understand Reddit content and display, train on, and otherwise use it.” Furthermore, Google states that this partnership does not affect its use of publicly accessible (crawl-able) content from the Internet for indexing, training or displaying such content in Google products.
Those partnerships mentioned above are the ones Google announced with named entities. However, those earlier posts did not provide sufficient technical information so as to allow comparison with the new pipeline. While the 2024 description notes “access to Reddit’s Data API,” the Oct. 8 posting describes approved platforms providing data through a Google ingestion pipeline. There was no reference to the Reddit partnership in the program page or the form.
As noted previously, one of the uses listed in the 2024 post is training. However, neither the program posting nor the posted application form referenced “training.”
There is a clear distinction between what has been published about the new program and the earlier partnerships. Google has made available to the general public both the eligibility criteria for participation in the new program and an online application. As previously discussed, Google provided identification of individual social platform partners through prior announcements.
Google’s support for the markup the program names predates it by almost three years. In November 2023, Google added discussion forum and profile page structured data , which I covered at the time . Google said the markup works with features “designed to show first-person perspectives from social media platforms, forums, and other communities,” and that using it “does not guarantee appearance.”
In June 2024, the changelog confirmed that SocialMediaPosting markup is also supported, “to more accurately reflect how the data ingestion for these features work.” In March 2026, Google added forum and Q&A properties “for providing more clarity on comment thread structure to Google ingestion systems.” The update included labels for AI-generated and bot content, which I covered in March .
Google’s current discussion forum markup page lists five interaction types it supports in interactionStatistic: likes or upvotes, dislikes or downvotes, views, comments, and reshares. The program page names the same markup, with interactionStatistic, as its example of what applicants should have on their pages.
Neither the forum documentation nor the program page says how Google uses those counts in ranking.
Google documents point to a separate intake for trending posts from forums and social platforms, apart from the crawling it uses for general web content. Approved platforms send the posts and their interaction signals themselves, while recrawl requests, sitemaps and the Indexing API all hand Google a URL to crawl.
Any platform that includes only feed items; requires login credentials for post views; or has user generated posts that cannot be linked back to a public profile does not qualify under the current specifications regardless of the size of their platform. The ten example URLs provided are intended to represent the format the platform plans to send to Google.
Whether or not the platform chooses to apply, the technical SEO can focus on the markup. Valid on-page structured data is one of the requirements, and in 2023 Google provided Search Console reporting and Rich Results Test support for both forum and profile markup. Those reports show errors, warnings, and valid items related to marked-up forum and profile pages.
If a site’s primary source of content is not user-generated content, then it fails the first qualification. However, these types of sites may still be competing against User Generated Content (Forum/Social) on the same searches, but Google did not name any participants. If you find your searches yielding more forum results, currently, there is no way within either the program page or form to determine whether the program is responsible for those increased results.
As of Oct. 15, none of the program page, form, or changelog entry (Oct. 8) names a participating platform. None of these items establish a numerical value for “a significant user base” despite this being one of the values requested via the Form to be reported as Monthly Active Users.
The program page references “various features on Search,” while the form says “Google Search and other surfaces.” They don’t identify a feature. The 72-hour counter window isn’t explained either.
The three listed documents also do not indicate how Google utilizes the interaction signals/engagement counts provided by participants; nor do they specify if participants will receive any reporting.
Applications are open through the form linked from the program page . Google says it will get back to applicants “within 6-8 weeks with a response on the status of your application.” Selected platforms then get “detailed technical integration documentation and onboarding instructions,” with no stated schedule for that step.
Google’s Search Central changelog records the Oct. 8 addition. It’s a place to watch for future changes to the documentation.
